transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. What brings you in to see me?

Hi, thank you for seeing me. Well, it's kind of hard to explain where it all started, but what finally made me actually pick up the phone and ask for help is that I just keep forgetting these little things. Things I normally handle without even thinking about it, you know? 

I work as a secretary, so my whole day is supposedly about keeping things on track, but I've been messing up the simplest stuff. Like, I'll mean to return a call—I'll look right at the message, or I'll see the missed call on my phone, and I'll think, "Okay, I'll call them right back after I finish this one thing," and then it just completely evaporates from my brain until hours later. Or turning in a registration form... I had this one form sitting in my bag for I don't even know how many days, just needing to be handed in, and I just kept forgetting it was there. 

And errands, oh my gosh, the errands. I'll be driving home from work, and the whole way I'm telling myself, "Stop at the store, stop at the store," and the next thing I know, I'm pulling into my own driveway and I completely forgot to stop on the way home. It's just these everyday little tasks that I should be able to do, and I usually *do* handle them, but lately it's just slipping right through my fingers and it's driving me absolutely crazy.
Have you always had this kind of forgetfulness since childhood, or is this a new change that started recently?

Oh, well... honestly, if I really sit down and think about it, it's definitely not new. I mean, I kept telling myself lately that maybe I'm just stressed or, I don't know, just having a busy month at the office, but no, it’s—it’s always been exactly like this. 

Even way back in elementary school, I was totally *that* kid. You know, the one who always forgot permission slips. I’d leave them sitting right on the kitchen counter, or worse, they’d get shoved into the very bottom of my backpack and just get completely crumpled up under my folders and gym clothes. My mom would find them weeks after the field trip already happened. And my homework, oh my gosh... I would actually do the work, sitting right there at the dining room table with my pencil and everything, but then it would just get lost in the black hole of my backpack and I'd never actually hand it in to the teacher. 

It was so frustrating, mostly for the adults around me, I think. My mom and my teachers basically had to tag-team just to get me through the week. If I had a project to do, like a diorama or a book report, they couldn't just tell me the due date and expect it to happen. They had to remind me step by step, every single day. They'd have to say, "Okay, did you get the poster board? Did you write the first paragraph? Did you glue the pictures on?" just to make sure I actually finished the thing. So, yeah, it’s not a new change at all. It’s just that now, as a 36-year-old woman, I don't have my mom or a teacher standing over my shoulder checking my bag, you know? So it feels like the consequences are so much bigger when I mess up at work, because there's nobody there to catch the things I drop.

latest_inference.note: Clear lifelong history of inattentive symptoms since childhood (forgotten permission slips, lost homework, needing external reminders) strongly supports predominantly inattentive ADHD. This rules out acute/adult-onset conditions like anxiety (F41.1), depression (F32.9), dementia (G30.9), acute stress reaction (F43.21), and nonspecific memory loss (R41.3), as the pattern is developmental rather than acquired or episodic.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a lifelong (since elementary school), pervasive pattern of inattentive symptoms—forgetfulness, losing/misplacing items, failing to complete or turn in tasks, difficulty sustaining attention to routine responsibilities—present both in childhood (school) and adulthood (work), causing functional impairment across settings. The chronicity since childhood, cross-situational presence, and predominance of inattentive symptoms without prominent hyperactive-impulsive behaviors support a diagnosis of Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, consistent with ICD-10 F90.0 (Disturbance of Activity and Attention).
